title: What's really in your perfume
whisper: a whale, a deer, a beaver and a ton of flowers
renderedWith: raea/sillage-notjustflowers (the map fields are unused; this file holds the script and the voice)

beats.say: Perfume isn't just flowers. Some of it came from a whale's gut.
It's called ambergris. A sperm whale makes it, and it can float at sea for years before it washes up.
Perfumers loved it because it makes a scent last on your skin.
Musk? It first came from a gland of the male musk deer. Since {1979|nineteen seventy-nine}, the deer is protected.
And the leather note in old classics? Castoreum. From beavers. Yes, beavers.
Here's the twist: today, almost all of these animal notes are made in a lab.
The flowers, though, are still real. And it takes a lot of them.
{1|One} kilo of jasmine oil needs about a ton of flowers, picked by hand around Grasse, France.
Most of the world's rose oil comes from two countries: Bulgaria and Turkey.
Vanilla is pollinated by hand, one flower at a time. An enslaved twelve-year-old, Edmond Albius, found the trick in {1841|eighteen forty-one}.
And about half the world's vetiver oil comes from Haiti. From the roots.
Whales, deer and beavers, rebuilt in a lab. A ton of flowers, picked by hand. That's what's in the bottle.
So next time you spray it, remember:
